passage:
Week one: Tanuja Ma'am noticed that Rafiq, who usually cracked jokes from the back row, had moved to a front corner and sat with his hood up. When a classmate teased him about his handwriting, he flushed and walked out. She let it go in class and later, privately, said, "You don't have to explain. I'm around if you want to talk."
Week three: Rafiq was eating lunch alone in the library. He answered her greeting with a shrug. She gave him a quiet job sorting books and didn't push.
Week five: The heaviness hadn't lifted. In an essay he wrote, "Everything feels grey and pointless lately." That same afternoon Tanuja gently asked if he would be okay with her talking to his parents and the school counsellor, Mr Thomas. He nodded. The counsellor saw Rafiq before home time, and Tanuja called his mother that evening.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq eating lunch in week three?
What was Tanuja feeling when she read Rafiq's essay line?
qa.a: She felt concerned, seeing that his sadness had lasted for weeks and was turning into hopelessness.

qa.q: Which choice in week five mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Gently involving his parents and the counsellor that same day, because lasting sadness and hopelessness need more than patience alone.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's quiet approach have felt to Rafiq?
qa.a: Probably safe and respectful; she gave him privacy and small tasks instead of pushing, so he could agree when she asked to involve others.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a cheerful student turn withdrawn and sensitive, offering patience and privacy, then involving family and a counsellor when sadness lasts.

passage: Darshan, you asked how to handle a student who suddenly goes quiet. Let me, Hemant, tell you about Revathi. Years ago she was in my Class Ten, the girl who argued with every poem. That winter she stopped arguing. She flinched when the boys teased her about her new glasses and fidgeted through lessons, tapping her pen till the bench shook. Some teachers called her moody. I gave her time and never questioned her in front of the class. But after some weeks she was still sitting alone at lunch, and one day she told me nothing felt worth trying anymore. That same day I spoke with her mother and walked Revathi to the counsellor's room myself. Years later she wrote to say that walk mattered.

qa.q: What were the boys teasing Revathi about?
What did Hemant feel when Revathi said nothing felt worth trying?
qa.a: Hemant felt worried enough to act that same day, seeing that her sadness had lasted and turned into hopelessness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Speaking with Revathi's mother and walking her to the counsellor that same day, because weeks of isolation and hopelessness needed more than patience.

qa.q: How might Revathi have experienced being called moody by some teachers?
qa.a: She probably felt misunderstood and more alone, when she actually needed patience and someone to notice her lasting sadness.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher seeing a lively student turn withdrawn and restless, giving patience and privacy, then bringing in family and a counsellor when sadness persists.
